A B S T R A C T
Electroless-plated cobalt alloys with tungsten typically exceeding 5 at.% are the common barrier materials for
copper metallization. As cobalt is a new interconnect material for advanced microchips, it is worth studying the
advanced cobalt-interconnect metallization process that involves extremely diluted cobalt-tungsten (CoW) alloys
with an eliminated impurity resistivity and enhanced electromigration reliability. To this aim, we fabricated
three different CoW nanolines with 0.03, 0.06 and 0.11 at.% of W using an electroless process, and examined
their electromigration behaviors under accelerated stressing conditions, using Co lines as a control. All three W
contents, especially 0.06 at.%, mitigate Co electromigration. The mechanism for the electromigration mitigation
is due to an improvement of the film s nanomechanical and surface wetting properties, as well as grain-structure
refinements. A full account of the relationship between the film properties, grain structures and electromigration
testing results is given, reasonably explaining the cause of the reliability optimization.

Current flow through a conductor under the action of an electric field
simultaneously places two forces on its atoms. One, the so-called direct
force, is the electrostatic force exerted by the electric field on the ion
cores, and another is the wind force due to the momentum transfer
between current-charge carriers (vastly electrons with an elementary
charge e) and the metal atoms [45]. As both forces are proportional to
the electric field E and a valence, the net electromigration force F is
conveniently related to the following equation:
F = (Z _ {d i r e c t} + Z _ {w i n d}) e E = Z * e E,\tag{3}
where
\mathbf { Z } _ { \mathrm { d i r e c t } }
is the nominal valence of the metal atoms (ignoring the
dynamic screening effect),
\mathbf { Z } _ { \mathrm { w i n d } }
is the electron-wind valence, and
stands for the effective valence. Electromigration involves diffusion of
metallic ions driven by the electromigration force F. Upon electro-
migration stressing, the ion diffusion is typically via a vacancy-transfer
mechanism with a flux J (in units of atoms cm
determined by the
atomic diffusivity
\mathbf { D } ,
the vacancy concentration
\mathrm { C } ,
the operating tem-
perature T, and the electromigration force F as:
J = D C / k T (Z *) e E\tag{4}
[46,47]. For the electrical stressing performed below half the abso-
lute melting point of a stressed metal, electromigration mass transport is
predominantly through grain boundaries (and interface) via a vacancy
diffusion mechanism.
The forced motion of metal atoms along their jump path towards
their neighboring vacancies leads to electromigration, eventually
causing the vacancies around the grain boundaries to deviate from the
equilibrium concentration. Assuming a negative effective valence, va-
cancies are depleted on the anode side and accumulated on the cathode
side of the grain boundaries [48,49].

there is a vacancy concentra-
tion gradient decreasing from cathode to anode. This gives rise to the
cathode side to have tensile forces and the anode side compressive
forces. The internal stress gradient in turn triggers atomic migration
opposing the electromigration atomic flux [31]. To account for this back
stress effect, a diffusion term has been included [8,50], and the total
electromigration flux is described as:
J (e m) = - D \partial C / \partial x + D C / k T (Z ^ {*}) e E.\tag{5}
Our experiments were made at ambient temperature being well
below half of the cobalt’s absolute melting point. Thus, the mass
transport of cobalt occurs primarily through the grain boundaries via a
vacancy diffusion mechanism. If the equilibrium of the total atomic flux,
as depicted in Eq. (5), is disturbed at triple points where grain bound
aries branch off, by the metal/substrate interfaces with existing strong
electron crowding effect, or by some inhomogeneous factors, such as
localized change in grain sizes [31,51], a divergence in the atomic or
vacancy flux will be present that creates extra vacancies for the nucle
ation of voids and subsequent growth of the voids in the surrounding
damaged area.
Here, the content of the W in Co is minor (0.03, 0.06 or 0.11 at.%),
and thus the effective valence
, diffusivity D and electrical resistivity ρ
of the alloyed Co are assumed to be the same as those of the unalloyed
Co. Stressing the Co and W-added Co lines with an identical current
density under the same temperature should induce the same electro-
migration flux at equilibrium according to Eq. (5). Thus, the reason for
the W-added Co lines to yield a higher resistance to a variety of flux
divergences showing a reduced void growth rate and extended electro-
migration lifetime, as implicitly confirmed by their smaller n factors, is
related to the higher film mechanical properties. As stated, compressive
and tensile stresses tend to build up, respectively, in the anode and
cathode sides of a damaged region around the grain boundaries or ma-
terial interfaces. The relaxation of the stress gradient by a back-diffusion
process accelerates the formation and growth of the voids there [52].

\mathbf { C o } ,

\mathrm { C o W } _ { \mathrm { m } } ,
